newsitem.title: UK: Oman sees telecoms reforms by 1998 -minister.
newsitem.headline: Oman sees telecoms reforms by 1998 -minister.

text.p: Reforms to Oman's telecommunications sector were likely to come into effect by 1998, a government minister said on Friday.
"By 1998 new providers may be allowed into the Oman telecoms market," minister of state for development affairs Mohamed Musa al-Yousef said at a press conference.
Yousef was in London to meet investors ahead of Oman's debut international bond issue, expected in the first week of March.
Last year the government said it would sell off between 10 and 15 percent of the government-owned General Telecommunication Organisation (GTO).
"We do not need to sell government assets to bring in money, and the idea behind (privatisation) is to reorganise the sector so the regulator and providor are split," Yousef said.
"At the moment the government is both, so we want to split these roles. Then we want to open up the sector to more providers," he said.
He said the government might also sell 15 percent of GTO stock to the public.
"(But) that is not the main point, we may or may not sell the stock. The key issue is opening up the sector and splitting the role of the regulator and the providers," Yousef said.
Other areas of privatisation included the electricity and water sectors, he said.
"Privatisation is not a big issue in Oman because there are not many companies to privatise. Our principle since the 1970s has been private sector-led development," Yousef said.
The exceptions were natural monopolies, like electricity and water, he said, but these were now being sold.
"Most of the (water and electricity) functions are managed by the private sector -- everything is contracted out although it is government owned," he said.
Oman was looking at creating a separate utility company in the south of the country, and had put out a tender for private electricity companies to take it over, he said.
Omani officials are traveling around the world in an effort to sell investors the country's first international bond issue.
Bankers said the five-year deal could be for at least $150 million. Yousef declined to comment on terms of the deal.
